title: Sabudana Kheer: The Creamy Fasting Dessert That Needs No Soaking
excerpt: This translucent tapioca-pearl kheer is a Navratri and vrat staple, but it works as an everyday dessert too — and a no-soak method cooks the pearls directly in water before the milk goes in.
body:
• Sabudana kheer — a creamy pudding of tapioca pearls, milk, sugar, cardamom and nuts — is a fasting staple during Navratri and other vrat days, and works as an everyday dessert too.
  • The no-soak method cooks the rinsed pearls directly in water first, since sabudana cooks faster in water than in milk — convenient when you have not planned ahead.
  • Fully cooked pearls are swollen and translucent with no hard white center; the kheer thickens as it cools, so keep it slightly thinner if serving chilled.
  • Video walkthrough for visual learners: Sabudana Kheer Recipe — Vrat Special Sweet by Life With Neha

Sabudana kheer is one of the most beloved fasting desserts in Indian homes: a creamy pudding of translucent tapioca pearls simmered in milk with cardamom, sugar and nuts. Families make it through Navratri, Ekadashi and Shivratri, but it doubles as a simple everyday dessert. The method below, adapted from Veg Recipes of India's family recipe, skips the usual hours-long soak — the rinsed pearls cook directly in water first, because sabudana softens faster in water than in milk.

The role of sabudana in vrat cooking

Sabudana, or sago, is made from the starch of the cassava root. Though it is not a grain, it has been accepted in fasting diets for generations across western and northern India, appearing in khichdi, vada and tikki during upvas days. During Navratri, when grains and legumes are avoided, sabudana dishes supply the starch and energy fasting households need. That is why sabudana kheer is frequently offered as bhog during Navratri, according to food writer Aditi Saraswat at Slurrp, who calls it "a good source of energy during fasting days and also for festive offerings."

"Though it is not a grain, it has been accepted in fasting diets for generations across western and northern India, appearing in khichdi, vada and tikki during upvas days."

Ingredients

  • ½ cup sabudana (regular tapioca pearls; avoid nylon sabudana)
  • 2 cups water
  • 2 cups whole milk
  • 4 to 5 tablespoons raw or white sugar, to taste
  • ½ teaspoon green cardamom powder (or 4–5 crushed green cardamoms)
  • 2 tablespoons chopped cashews
  • ½ tablespoon raisins
  • 3 to 4 saffron strands, for garnish (optional)

Method

  1. Rinse the sabudana under running water a few times until the water runs clear, draining away excess starch. Drain well, then transfer to a thick-bottomed pan with 2 cups of fresh water. No soaking is needed.
  2. Cook the sabudana on low to medium heat, stirring at intervals so the pearls do not stick. After 5 to 6 minutes the pearls will begin to float, swell and turn translucent — they have started cooking but are not fully soft yet. Meanwhile, warm 2 cups of milk in a separate pan (do not boil it).
  3. Add the warm milk and the cardamom powder to the sabudana. Mix well.
  4. Add the sugar and simmer for 20 to 25 minutes on low to medium heat, stirring often so the milk and pearls do not stick or scorch. If the kheer thickens too much before the pearls are done, add a little warm milk. Taste a few pearls: they should be swollen, translucent and completely soft, with no hard or chewy white center.
  5. Keep the consistency slightly thinner than you want, especially if serving chilled — the kheer thickens considerably as it cools, and some pearls break down, naturally thickening the milk.
  6. Turn off the heat and stir in the cashews and raisins. Taste and add more sugar if needed.
  7. Serve hot, warm or chilled, garnished with saffron strands or chopped nuts. If it has thickened too much after cooling, stir in a little milk to loosen it.

Tips for the perfect texture

The single most common mistake is undercooked pearls — a dense white center means more simmering time, not more heat. Use regular-sized sabudana rather than nylon sabudana, whose texture and cooking time differ. Full-fat milk gives the creamiest result; for a plant-based version, cook the sabudana completely in water first, then add almond or coconut milk and heat gently without boiling. If you prefer jaggery over sugar, add it only after turning off the heat and letting the kheer cool for 4 to 5 minutes — boiling milk with jaggery can curdle it.

Store leftovers in a covered container in the refrigerator and consume within 2 days. Do not freeze: freezing and thawing changes the texture of both the milk and the pearls.

A note for diaspora kitchens

Small tapioca pearls are stocked in nearly every Indian grocery store in the US, UK and Canada, usually shelved near the poha and rice flour. The no-soak method matters most abroad: when Navratri falls on a workday, you can start the kheer in the evening without having planned hours ahead. A plain steel pan on low heat and a wooden spoon are all the equipment this needs.
